translations.text: A sermon by John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople, for Holy Thursday: on Judas’s betrayal, on the Passover [?], on the explanation of the holy mysteries, and on not bearing grudges.
Today I must speak briefly to you, my beloved. I must speak briefly, not because you find the abundance of what is said burdensome.
For no other city can be found that devotes itself so lovingly to hearing spiritual words.
But there is a pressing reason for speaking briefly today: I see many of the faithful approaching to partake of the awe-inspiring mysteries.
So that they may neither miss the one table nor be deprived of the other, we must prepare a meal today, so that perhaps you may benefit from both.
Having had your fill of this table and of our words, you will then depart and approach the awe-inspiring and fearsome Communion with fear and trembling and with fitting self-restraint.
For today, beloved, our Lord Jesus was betrayed.
Rather, grieve and weep bitterly, not for Jesus who was betrayed, but for Judas who betrayed him.
For Jesus, who was betrayed, saved the whole world, but Judas, who betrayed him, destroyed his own soul.
The one who was betrayed sits at the Father’s right hand in heaven, but the one who betrayed him is now in Hades. Eternal
torment is what he awaits. Groan for him; weep for him, since our Lord himself wept for him.
For when he saw him, he was troubled and said, declaring, “One of you will betray me.” Why was he sorrowful?
And he showed his love, teaching us that we should always mourn not the person who suffers harm, but the person who does evil.
For this is worse than the other—or rather, suffering evil is not evil, but doing evil is evil.

For suffering evil wins the kingdom of heaven for us, while doing evil makes us liable to eternal fire and torment. For he said, “Blessed are those chosen for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Do you see that suffering evil has as its reward and gift the kingdom of heaven? Hear how doing evil brings torment and suffering. For after Paul said of the Jews that they killed the Lord and drove away the prophets, he added their end: “It will be according to their deeds.” Do you see how those who are persecuted receive the kingdom, while those who persecute receive wrath? I have not said this now without a purpose, but so that we may not be angry with our enemies, but have mercy on them, weep for them, and care for them. For those who are hostile to us are themselves the ones suffering harm. If we put our souls in this condition, we can also pray for them. This is why I have now been speaking with you for four days about prayer for enemies, so that the message of this teaching may become firmly established, as through repeated instruction it is

taken in. This is why we repeatedly wash you with words, so that we may soothe and restrain the fierceness of anger, and so that whoever comes to prayer may be free of anger. For Christ taught this not only for our enemies’ sake, but also for our own sake, as we forgive them their sins. You will receive more than your enemy does if you give—if you forgive your enemy’s sin. “How, then, will I receive more?” he says. Forgive your enemy’s sins, and you will be forgiven for what you have sinned against the Master. Those sins are without healing and without mercy, while these have great consolation and mercy. So listen to Eli speaking to his sons, if they have sinned [?]: “If a man sins against another man, prayer is offered for him. But if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” Thus not even prayer readily soothes that wound. Prayer does not soothe it, but forgiving your enemy’s sins does soothe it. That is why God called those sins against the Master ten thousand talents, but these a hundred denarii. Forgive the hundred denarii, so that you may be forgiven the ten thousand talents.

Now we have spoken enough about prayer. Let us turn again to the betrayal and see how our Master was betrayed. “Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said, ‘What will you give me, and I will betray him to you?’” I think the meaning of these words is clear and needs no further defense. But if someone carefully examines each
of the things related, it has many aspects and a great depth of meaning.
First, the time. For the evangelist did not indicate it without a purpose. He did not simply say, “He went,”
but added, “Then he went.” Then—when? Tell me. And why does he indicate the time? What are you to learn? The word “then” was not spoken to you without a purpose. He speaks by the Spirit.
And whoever speaks by the Spirit says nothing without a purpose or without understanding. What, then, does “then” mean? Before that time, before that hour,
a prostitute came carrying a flask of fragrant ointment, and she poured that olive oil over the Lord’s head. She showed great faith.
She showed great healing, great obedience and self-control. She turned away from this passing life and became better and wiser. And when the prostitute repented, when she recognized the Master,
then the disciple betrayed his teacher.
That is why he said “then”: so that you would not accuse the teacher of weakness when you saw the disciple betraying him. For so great was the teacher’s power
that he could draw even a prostitute into obedience to him. What, then? Did he draw the prostitute to himself but lack the power to draw the disciple?
He could have drawn the disciple too, but he did not wish to make him good by force
or draw him to himself by compulsion. “Then he went.” These words, “he went,” also have no small significance. For he did not say that he was summoned by the chief priests or compelled,
but that, without compulsion, he acted on his own. At home he conceived his evil deceit and devised his plan, without having a single adviser
or friend. “Then one of the twelve went.” What does “one of the twelve” mean? This too shows his great [?], by saying, “one of the twelve.”
For Jesus also had other disciples, seventy in number. But they were of the second rank.
They did not have so much honor, nor so much freedom of speech, nor did they share in so many mysteries. These twelve were chosen above the rest, and that is what these were.
the company gathered around the teacher. And Judas broke away from them.
But so that you would learn that it was not an ordinary disciple of his who betrayed him, but one of the chosen company, he said, “one of the twelve.”
And Matthew is not ashamed to write this.
Why is he not ashamed? So that you would learn that everywhere they tell the whole truth and conceal nothing, not even things that might seem disgraceful.

For this very thing that seems disgraceful shows the Master’s love for humanity: he counted a traitor, a robber, a thief worthy of such great blessings, and continued to bear patiently with him until the last evening.

For he instructed him and taught him and cared for him in every way. So do not despair of yourself when you look at the prostitute, nor, again, put your trust in yourself when you look at Judas. For both are ruinous: self-confidence and despair. Self-confidence makes the one who stands fall, while despair does not allow the one who lies fallen to rise. That is why Paul teaches, saying:

Let anyone who thinks he stands take care not to fall. You have an example of both: how the disciple who thought he stood fell, and how the prostitute who lay fallen rose. Our mind is slippery; our thought is unstable. For this reason we must strengthen and guard ourselves everywhere, on every side. Then one of the Twelve, Judas Iscariot, went away. Do you see from what a position he fell? Do you see how much teaching he disregarded? Do you see how great an evil laziness and coldness are? Judas, who was called Iscariot. Why do you tell me his town?

[?] I wish I did not even know him—Judas, called Iscariot. Why, then, does he tell us his town? There was another disciple named Judas, called the Zealot. To prevent their having the same name from causing any confusion, he distinguished this one from the other. He identified the other by his goodness: Judas the Zealot. But he did not identify this one by his wickedness, for he did not say, “Judas the betrayer,” although it would have been fitting, just as he named the other for his virtue, to name this one for his wickedness and say, “Judas the betrayer.” But to teach you to keep your tongue free of slander, he hesitates even over the betrayer himself. Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests and said to them, “What are you willing to give me, and I will betray him to you?” Oh, that disgusting utterance! How did it leap from his mouth? How did he move his tongue? How did his body not become entirely

numb? How did he not lose his mind? “What are you willing to give me, and I will betray him to you?” Tell me, was this what your teacher taught you? Was it not for this reason that he said, “Do not acquire gold,

or silver, or copper for your belts”? From the mountain he had already [?] instructed you about the love of money. Was this not what he always taught? And afterward he said, “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well.” “What are you willing to give me?” What madness! “And I will betray him to you.” Tell me, for what? What charge, small or great, do you have against your teacher, that you betray him? Is it because he gave you authority over demons? Because he enabled you to cure diseases? Because he enabled you to cleanse lepers? Because he enabled you to raise the dead? Because he placed you above the power of death? Is this the repayment you give for these kindnesses? “What are you willing to give me, and I will betray him to you?” Oh, the madness—or rather, oh, the love of money! For it produced all this evil. With his thoughts fixed on it, this man betrayed his teacher. For such is that evil root,

more savage than a demon, throwing the souls it has ensnared into turmoil. It makes a person forget everything: himself, his neighbors, and the laws of nature. It drives him out of his very self and makes him senseless. Look how much it drove out of Judas’s soul then: their conversations, their familiar companionship, their fellowship at the table, the miracles, the teaching, the counsel, the instruction—all these

Love of money then made him forget. Thus Paul rightly said, “The love of money is the root of all evil.” “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” What great madness in these words! Tell me, are you handing over the one who holds all things together, who rules over demons, who rebukes the sea, the Lord of all creation? But to restrain his madness and teach him that, unless he himself were [?], he would not have given himself up, listen to what he does at the very time when he gives himself up.
When they came against him with clubs and torches, he said to them, “Whom are you looking for?” And they did not recognize the one they wanted to seize.
So powerless was Judas to hand him over that he did not even see the one he wanted to betray standing there, although there were torches and so much light.
For the evangelist emphasized this when he said, “They had torches, and it was light, yet they did not see him.”
For he continually reminded him each day, showing by deeds and words that the betrayer would not escape.
So he did not openly expose him before everyone, so that he would not make him more shameless.
Nor did he keep silent, so that Judas would not think he was escaping notice and begin to betray him without fear. He often said, "One of you will betray me," but he did not openly point him out.

He also spoke at length about the day of judgment, and at length about the kingdom of heaven. He showed his power in both respects: to punish those who had sinned and to honor those who had walked uprightly.
But Judas disregarded all this, and God did not draw him by force.
For since he gave us the power to do both evil and good deeds, he wants us to be good of our own free will.
Therefore, if we are unwilling, he does not compel us. For being good under compulsion is not goodness.
For Judas too was master of his own mind, and of his own free will he refused to listen, turning instead to the love of money.
Because of this he became blind in his mind and betrayed his own Savior, saying, “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?”
Thus, exposing his madness, the evangelist said, “At the time of their arrival, Judas was standing near them”—the one who had said:
“What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” Yet Christ’s power can be seen not only from this, but also from the fact that, when he uttered a quiet word,

they went away. But since even in this way they did not come to feel shame, he voluntarily gave himself up [?], all but saying, “I have done everything on my part. I have revealed my power; I have shown that you are attempting deeds beyond your strength.
I wanted to restrain your wickedness. But since you are unwilling and still persist in your wickedness, look, I give myself up.”
I have explained this to you so that no one may slander Christ by saying, “Why did he not turn Judas toward goodness? Why did he not make him wise and gentle?”
But how was he to make Judas gentle: by force or by free will?
If by force, even so Judas was unwilling to become better. No one becomes good through compulsion. But if by free will, it is possible to set everything right: free will had been given to him.
And if he did not wish to accept the herbs as a help, the fault is not the physician's,
but belongs to the one who did not wish to be healed. Look how much he did to turn him, to save him from that. He taught him all wisdom, by both deeds and words.
He made him higher than the demons. He gave him power to work many miracles. He frightened him with the fire to come. He won him over with the promise of the kingdom. He often exposed his thoughts.

And again, while he rebuked him, he did not expose him. He washed his feet along with the others, and admitted him to the table and to communion. Nothing was lacking to him, small or great. But he chose to remain in perdition. And so that you may learn that he was able to change but did not wish to, and that everything came about through his own sloth: when he had betrayed him, he threw down the thirty denarii, and what did he say? "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood." What happened when he saw him working miracles? He did not say, "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood," but, "What will you give me, and I will betray him to you?" When the evil had been carried out, the betrayal had reached its end and the sin had been completed, then he understood the sin. What, then, do we learn from this?
That when we are lazy, no

instruction profits us. But when we exert ourselves and move ourselves to the good, it does. This man did not listen when the teacher was instructing him. But when no one was instructing him, he then recognized his own conscience. With no teacher present, he changed, repented of his reckless deeds, and threw down the thirty pieces of silver. "What will you give me, and I will betray him to you?" And they set thirty pieces of silver for him. They set a price on blood that has no price. Why do you take thirty pieces of silver, O Judas? Christ came freely to shed his blood for the whole world, and you are bargaining over that blood and making an exchange, you shameless one. For what is more shameless than this exchange? "Then the disciples came." Then: when? When this happened, when the betrayal had been carried out, when Judas had destroyed himself, his disciples came to him, saying to him: "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?"

He saw the disciples; he saw the disciple. That one betrays the Master, and these are concerned about serving him. That one makes a plot, and these prepare to serve. Both these and that one had the same things: the same miracles, the same teachings, the same instruction. Where, then, did the change come from? From the will: that is the whole cause, in everything, for both good and evil. "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?"

[?]: It was then evening. Since the Master had no house, they therefore say: "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?" I have no fixed lodging, I have neither dwelling nor house. Let those who build splendid houses, spacious porches and long courtyards learn that Christ had nowhere to lay his head. So these men ask, "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?" Which Passover? Not this Passover, but the Jewish one. Still, that is the one the disciples prepared.

And he himself established this Passover of ours; indeed, he himself became the Passover. "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?" That was the Jewish Passover; that one had its beginning in Egypt. Why, then, did Christ eat that Passover? Because he fulfilled everything that the law required. For when he was being baptized he said: "For thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness." "I came," he says, "to redeem man from the curse of the law." For God sent his own Son, born of a woman, born under the law, so that he might redeem those under the law and bring the law itself to rest. But let no one say that he abolished the law and brought it to an end because he could not fulfil it, as though it were too heavy. He first fulfilled all of it, and then he dissolved it. This is why he also kept the Passover. Of the law [?]...

a commandment was the Passover. And why did the law command that the Passover be eaten? The Jews were unmindful of their benefactor and at once forgot the benefactions of God their protector. For indeed, when they had come out of Egypt and had seen the sea part and close again, and many other wonders, they said: "Make us gods who will go before us."
What are you saying? While you are still holding the wonders in your hand, have you so forgotten God your benefactor?
Since they were so unfeeling and ignorant, God tied the remembrance of his gifts to the festivals.
For this reason he commanded them to sacrifice the Passover lamb. “If your son asks you,” he said, “what this Passover means,”
you shall say this: “The children smeared the doors with sheep’s blood in Egypt.
Then the destroyer came, and when he saw it, he did not dare rush in and bring the plague. And the feast was a perpetual remembrance of their deliverance.
But this was not its only benefit for them—that it reminded them of former blessings. There was another, greater benefit: it showed them beforehand what was to come.

For was not that lamb a symbol of another lamb, a spiritual one? One was a sheep, and the other was a sheep. But one was a shadow, and the other was the reality. Once the true sun appeared, the shadow began to disappear.
When the sun rises, the shadow disappears.
For this reason both Passovers took place at that table: the figurative one and the true one.
For just as painters draw outlines and paint the finished image in color on the same panel, so Christ did at that table.
He sketched the symbolic Passover and added the true one. “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
It was the Jewish Passover. But once the sun has come, let the light no longer shine. Once the reality has come, the shadow serves no purpose.
I say these things to the Jews, since they think they are celebrating the Passover, since with shameful minds they set out unleavened bread, though they are always uncircumcised in heart.
Tell me, how do you celebrate the Passover?
O Jew, the temple has been torn down, the altars demolished, the Holy of Holies closed off, and every sacrificial offering has ceased. Why do you dare to engage in these unlawful deeds?
You once went to Babylon, and there those who had taken you captive said, “Sing us a song of the Lord,” and you could not.
And David, showing this, said: “By the river of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion.
“On the willows in its midst we hung our instruments”—that is, harps, flutes, pipes, and the rest. For these were used under the old covenant, and with them they sang songs.
And when they went into captivity, they took these with them to preserve the memory of life in their own land, but not to sing.
“For there,” it says, “those who had taken us captive asked us for the words of songs.” We said, “How can we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”
What are you saying? You do not sing the Lord’s songs in a foreign land?
Yet you celebrate the Lord’s Passover in a foreign land? Do you see the folly? Do you see the lawlessness?

When wars were putting them under compulsion, they could not even sing songs in a foreign land. But now, with no one compelling them or causing them distress, they wage war against God. Do you see how impious the feast of Unleavened Bread is, how lawless the festival is, how the Passover is no longer Jewish? There was once a Jewish Passover, but now it has been abolished, and the spiritual Passover has come, which he handed down then. For while they were eating and drinking, he took bread, broke it, and said, “This is my body, broken for you.” Those who have been instructed know what is being said. And again, taking the cup, he said, “This is my blood, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.” And Judas came while Christ was saying this. This is the blood, Judas, which you sold for thirty denarii.

This is the blood for whose sake you so often held those shameful consultations with the foolish Pharisees. How great is Christ’s love for humanity! How great is Judas’s lawlessness! How great his madness! For he sold it for thirty denarii, yet even after this Christ did not refuse to give this blood that had been sold for the forgiveness of sins, if only he had been willing. For he came

—Judas—to partake of the holy table. For just as he washed his feet when he washed those of the other disciples, so he also gave him the holy offerings, so that he would have no excuse at all if he persisted in evil. For Christ did everything that was his to do, but Judas nevertheless persisted in his evil purpose. But now it is time to approach this exalted table. Let us all therefore go with fitting self-restraint and purity. Let no one there be a Judas. Let no one be evil. Let no one harbor poison. Let no one have one thing on his lips and another in his mind.

Christ has come, and he is the same even now. The one who prepared that table also prepares this one now. For it is not a human being who makes the things set before us become Christ’s body and blood, but Christ, who was crucified for us. The priest carries out his role, speaking those words, but the power and the gift are entirely God’s. “This is my body,” he said. This word transforms the things set before us. And just as that utterance, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth,” was spoken once, yet remains effective throughout all ages, empowering our nature to bear offspring, so this utterance, spoken once, continually brings about the perfect sacrifice at the table in the churches, from that time until today and until his coming. Therefore let no one come with deceit. Let no one come full of malice [?]. Let no one harbor poison
...in mind, so that he may not receive condemnation. For at that time, when Judas also took the bread,

then the devil leapt into him. He did this not out of contempt for the Lord's body but out of contempt for Judas's shamelessness. This is so that you may learn that the devil leaps into and enters more often into those who receive the holy communion unworthily, just as he did into Judas then. For to the worthy these things flow purely, but they cast those who receive them unworthily into greater torment. And I do not say this to frighten you, but rather to strengthen you. Let no one here be a Judas and carry the poison of evil. The sacrifice is spiritual food. Bodily food that falls into a stomach full of bad humours makes the illness last longer, not because of its own nature but because of the stomach's sickness. It is the same with the spiritual mysteries. When these fall into a mind full of malice, they harm and destroy it all the more, not because of their own nature but because of the sickness of the soul that received them.
So let no one keep an evil mind within himself. Instead, let us purify our hearts, for we are coming to a pure sacrifice. Let us make our souls holy, for this can happen in a single day.
How, and in what way? If you have something against your enemy, tear out your anger.
Heal the wound and put an end to the enmity, so that you may receive healing from the table. You are coming to a dread and holy sacrifice. Fear what is told of that offering. Slain [?]...
Christ lies before you.

For this reason he was slain. And why? To reconcile the things of heaven, to make you a friend of the angels, and for Christ to reconcile you completely to God. To unite you with both the angels and the Lord of the angels, he gave his own life, although you were an enemy and an adversary.
Yet you hold back from your fellow servant, clinging to hostility.
How can you approach the Lord’s table of peace? He did not refuse to die for you, yet you are unwilling even to let go of your anger against your fellow servant.
"For he did me great harm," he says, "and wore me out badly." So what? Even if you suffered a great loss of property, he never crucified you.
as the Jews crucified Christ. Yet he himself gave the very blood that they shed for the salvation of those who shed it.
What can you say to this in reply? If you do not give up your enmity toward your enemy, it is not him you have harmed.
but rather yourself. For you have often harmed him in this life, but you have also made the answer you must give on the day of judgment one that will receive no mercy.
God hates nothing so much as a person who holds a grudge, for this is a heart inflamed and a soul swollen with pride.
Listen to what he said: “When you bring your gift to the altar and there, standing before the altar, remember
that your brother has something against you, leave your gift and go and be reconciled with your brother.”

What are you saying? ‘Am I to forgive?’ ‘Yes,’ he said. For this sacrifice too is for reconciliation with your brother. Yet you do not establish peace, and still you partake of the sacrifice. But you have not understood what it accomplished. First, therefore, do that for which the sacrifice was offered, and then you will be well satisfied. For this is why the Son of God came down: to reconcile our nature to God. For this reason he not only came himself, but also promised that we who do the same would share the title of his own name. For he said, ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.’ For what the only-begotten Son of God did,

...You too will do this as far as you are able, becoming a mediator of peace both for yourself and for us. This is why he calls you a son of God, the peacemaker. This is why, at the time of the sacrifice (the text reads "harvest" [?]), he mentioned no other righteousness separately, but only that we should have peace with everyone, showing that this is greater than everything else. I wanted to make my sermon longer, but what has been said is enough for those who pay attention, if they remember it. So let us always remember these words about the holy kisses, the dread embrace that we give one another. For this binds our minds together and makes all of us into one body, since we also share in one flesh. So let us all be joined into one body, not by fleshly

mingling with one another, but by binding our souls together in the bond of love. In this way we can be fully satisfied from the table that lies before us. For even if we have countless righteous deeds to our credit, if we remember the wrongs done to us,
all of it is worthless and in vain, and none of it can produce the fruit of salvation. Knowing this, let us put away all anger and cleanse our consciences, and with all meekness and gentleness...
let us approach the table of Christ, with whom glory belongs to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit,
now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
